title: Downfall
hookLine: a shining visitor asks, again and again: and what is the next cause of downfall?

cards: Nobody wakes up one morning and decides to wreck their life. It goes slower than that. A habit here, a skipped call to a parent there, a little more money spent than earned, a little more pride than the situation needed.
Years later, it adds up. The sixth poem of the Sutta Nipata is a slow-motion map of that slide.
Late at night, a shining deity lights up the grove where the Buddha is staying, asks one question, then keeps coming back with the same follow-up: that's one. Tell me the next.

teach.h: THE ONE WHO RISES IS EASY TO KNOW
teach.b: The poem is the Parabhava Sutta, the discourse on downfall, or decline. It opens simply: the one who rises is easy to know, and the one who falls is easy to know.
Whoever loves the good teaching rises; whoever hates it falls.
Then the visitor asks for the next cause, and the next, about a dozen in all. Some sound ancient, addressed to a man of that time. But many land today.
Keeping company with bad people and liking their ways. Loving sleep, loving crowds, never making an effort, quick to anger. Being able to support your aging mother and father, and not doing it.
Lying to a holy person to deceive them. Having plenty of wealth and good food, and eating it alone. Being proud of your family, your money or your name, and looking down on your own relatives.
Drinking, gambling, chasing affairs, and losing what you earn. Putting a reckless spender in charge of your affairs. Having little and wanting a throne.
Notice what's barely on the list: ritual.

Apart from the first verse, about the teaching itself, and a few on sloth and appetite, the causes are ways of treating people: parents, relatives, the hungry, the trusting. Downfall here is mostly relational.

teach.h: NOT RICH: RICH AND EATING ALONE
teach.b: And one quiet detail: the wealthy person isn't condemned for being wealthy, only for eating alone.
The poem closes: the wise, seeing these causes of downfall clearly, take the safe road.

how: The Parabhava Sutta is among the protective discourses chanted in Theravada communities, and it is often taught to lay Buddhists as practical advice on family, money and friendship.

o: a sudden ruin sent as a punishment
losing your fortune by bad luck
a slow slide, a person's decline

games.q: causes of downfall: tap the pairs.

s: it names eating your good food alone, not wealth itself.
the visitor keeps asking for the next cause
the poem is built on that repeated question, about a dozen times.
most causes in the poem are about missed rituals
almost all are about how we treat people: parents, relatives, the hungry.

games.q: you have plenty of money and a table full of good food. which does the poem name as a cause of downfall?
o: eating the good food by yourself.
games.why: the poem names the wealthy person who enjoys delicacies alone: the problem is not sharing.

practice: Go through the list quietly, bad company, too much sleep, a parent who needs a call, a meal not shared, pride in front of family, money leaking away, and notice which sits closest to your life right now, without judging yourself.
Then picture one small step away from it, a call, a shared plate, an early night, and hold that picture for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: Downfall. The Parabhava Sutta: about a dozen ways a person slowly falls, almost all of them about how we treat the people around us. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali parabhava: decline, downfall, ruin. the name of Sn 1.6.

carryVoice: Your line: causes of downfall. Most of them are about how we treat each other. Day five hundred eighty-three, done.
